A.explanation: Shows straight wavefronts continuing through the gap with no spreading, so no diffraction is shown and wavelength appears changed.

B.explanation: Shows some curvature but the diffracted wavefronts do not spread out into wide circular arcs centred at the narrow gap.

C.explanation: Shows plane waves spreading through a gap of width similar to $\lambda$ into circular arcs centred at the gap with unchanged spacing.

D.explanation: Shows curved wavefronts that are not centred at the gap, so they do not represent diffraction originating from the gap.

hints: Notice the incident straight plane wavefronts on the left and the narrow gap in the vertical barrier whose width is similar to the incident wavelength.
Recall that diffraction is spreading of waves through a gap, with maximum spreading when gap width is about equal to wavelength $\lambda$.
Check which diagram keeps the same wavefront spacing $\lambda$ after the barrier but changes straight lines into wide circular arcs centred at the gap.
walkthrough: Identify the set-up: straight plane water wavefronts travel to the right towards a barrier with a small gap whose width is comparable to the wavelength $\lambda$.
State the rule: diffraction is the spreading of waves at a gap or edge, strongest when gap width is of order $\lambda$, and the wave speed and wavelength $\lambda$ do not change.

Therefore the transmitted waves should originate at the gap and spread into the region behind the barrier as circular arcs centred on the gap, with the same separation $\lambda$ as the incident waves.
Compare the diagrams: A shows almost straight short dashes with no spreading, B shows only slight local curvature, and D shows arcs not centred at the gap.
Only the diagram with wide semicircular wavefronts centred at the gap and with unchanged spacing satisfies both spreading and constant $\lambda$. This is option C.
